title: The hilltop mansion that blocked a park

place.label: Hilltop of Lafayette Park, site of the Holladay mansion

hook: For seventy years a lawyer's private mansion sat at the top of a public park. The Depression finally cleared it away.
story: Samuel Wirt Holladay was a lawyer who, as city attorney from 1860 to 1863, had defended San Francisco's claims to public land. Then he challenged the city's claim to this hill under the 1855 Van Ness Ordinance [1]. He fenced six parcels between Gough and Octavia, dug a well in 1869 and built an Italianate mansion with a water tower. By one account Bret Harte, Mark Twain and Leland Stanford visited [1]. The legal fight lasted seventy years, mostly in Holladay's favour. The empty house later grew eerie with neglect [1]. Developer Louis Lurie bought it in the 1920s and pushed to run Clay Street through the park to reach an apartment building he planned. Neighbours and Park Commissioners led by Herbert Fleishhacker fought him off, and in 1935 he sold the land to the city [1]. Between 1936 and 1938 WPA crews put in more than 100,000 hours of work. They demolished the mansion and water tower but kept the estate's old paths and stairs, and made the spot where the house stood into a play area for mothers and small children [1]. One private building survived: the St. Regis apartments on Gough Street, still the only privately owned building in a San Francisco public park [2].

title: The city's first foreign-film cinema
hook: A Fillmore nickelodeon became San Francisco's first foreign-film house, then a midnight-movie shrine. Several of the best stories about it turned out to be untrue.
story: The little cinema at 2261 Fillmore opened in 1913 as the Regent, showing Mary Pickford films. In 1935 it reopened as the Clay-International. The city's historic review later confirmed that it was San Francisco's first theatre dedicated to foreign films, and a major art-house screen until the late 1980s [1]. Later it became a midnight-movie institution, known for The Rocky Horror Picture Show and The Room [2]. In 1985 it even hosted the world premiere of the western spoof Lust in the Dust, with Divine in attendance [2]. The landmark review also punctured some local legends. The Clay did not open in 1910, and it did not show San Francisco's first midnight movie with Pink Flamingos in 1972, a claim John Waters himself had repeated. Pink Flamingos reached the Clay in 1974 [1]. Landmark Theatres ran the cinema from 1991 [2]. It showed its last film on January 26, 2020: a midnight Rocky Horror [1]. In April 2022 the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to make it a landmark [1]. In 2025 venture capitalist Neil Mehta, who had been buying up Fillmore Street properties, announced plans to reopen it as a 200-seat repertory cinema [3].

title: A marble mansion given to the nuns

place.label: Flood Mansion, Convent of the Sacred Heart, 2222 Broadway

hook: In 1939 a widow gave away her marble mansion with its Golden Gate view. Within a year, 97 schoolgirls and 25 nuns had moved in.
story: In June 1939 the Society of the Sacred Heart learned that Maud Lee Flood wanted to give them her family home: a marble mansion on the Broadway ridge that looked out over the Bay and the newly finished Golden Gate Bridge [1]. Her husband had died and her children had grown up and left, and she wanted the house to have a purpose. So she handed it over to Reverend Mother Eleanor Deming [1]. The family drawing room became a chapel. At the start of 1940 about 25 nuns, seven lay teachers and 97 students moved in [1]. Mrs. Flood wrote that she was pleased the house of "happy and unforgettable memories" had become "a house of learning, refinement, and peace" [1]. The war changed the school too: many families wanted their sons and daughters in one school, so boys joined the lower grades [1]. When the Grant mansion next door came up for sale, the nuns had already slipped religious medals onto its grounds through the latticework. The family sold it to them for $150,000. The school gives 1950 as the year, while NoeHill says 1948 [1][2]. In 1956 the Society bought Hammond House on the other side, and Stuart Hall for Boys opened there with 42 boys [1].

title: Hitler's captain on Jackson Street
hook: In the spring of 1941 a sandstone mansion on Jackson Street became Nazi Germany's San Francisco consulate. Its consul had been Hitler's commanding officer in the First World War.
story: William Franklin Whittier's Arizona sandstone mansion was built between 1894 and 1896 [2]. In April 1941 it passed in quick steps from the family to a title company, then to Herman Loeper on April 28, then to "Das Deutsches Reich" the next day [1]. The Chronicle later reported that the price was $44,000 [3]. The consul general was Fritz Wiedemann, whom a 1937 Chronicle headline had called "Hitler's War Captain" [3]. According to the federal architectural survey, he entertained elegantly while carrying out secret Nazi business, including trying to pressure German-Americans into "serving the party" [1]. Staff piled filing cabinets in the old dining room, and his family lived on the third floor [3]. In July 1941 he was ordered to leave. A stove near the furnace is thought to have been used to burn documents [1]. After a false start via Japan, the consular party flew to New York and sailed home via Portugal [1][3]. The US government seized the house, which stood shut through the war. In March 1950 it was auctioned [1]. It later housed Mortimer Adler's Institute for Philosophical Research and, from 1956, the California Historical Society [2].

title: A car jack from Fillmore Street

place.label: Former Stanford hospital campus, Clay Street near Webster

hook: The first medical linear accelerator in the Western Hemisphere saved a small boy's sight in a Pacific Heights hospital, with help from a jack borrowed from a local garage.
story: In the 1950s Stanford's medical school still stood on Clay Street, next to the old Lane Hospital [3]. Its radiology chief, Henry Kaplan, heard at cocktail parties about the atom smasher that physicists on the Palo Alto campus were building. He and physicist Edward Ginzton turned it into a cancer-treatment machine. It was the first medical linear accelerator in the Western Hemisphere, installed at Stanford-Lane Hospital in San Francisco [1]. In January 1956 it treated its first patient, a boy with a tumour, a retinoblastoma, in his one remaining eye. Stanford's 2007 account says he was two, while a faculty memorial of Kaplan says he was a seven-month-old baby [1][2]. The lead shielding needed a steady mount. Kaplan remembered "the puzzled look on the face of the garage owner down on Fillmore Street" when he asked to borrow a heavy-duty car jack. It held a block of lead with a pinhole, lined up day after day for six weeks with the tumour while missing the lens and cornea [1]. The boy kept his sight [1]. The machine treated patients for 16 years before going to the Smithsonian in 1972 [1]. Kaplan also pushed, over strong opposition, to move the medical school out of San Francisco to the Palo Alto campus [2].

title: Sinatra's nightclub in a sugar palace
hook: In Pal Joey the limestone palace of sugar heir Adolph Spreckels played Frank Sinatra's nightclub. The real owner was a former artist's model from the sand dunes.
story: In the 1957 film Pal Joey, the French Baroque mansion at 2080 Washington Street played Chez Joey, Frank Sinatra's nightclub [1]. George Applegarth designed it in 1912 for sugar heir Adolph Spreckels and his wife Alma de Bretteville [1]. Alma was born in the Sunset District to poor Danish immigrants and modelled for local artists. Robert Aitken used her as the model for the figure on top of the Dewey Monument in Union Square [1]. She married Adolph in 1908. He died in 1924, and she stayed on in the house [1]. It became her base for charity work. During the Second World War its huge garage served as a recycling centre and air-raid shelter. A thrift shop that raised money for the Legion of Honor, the museum she founded, ran there until 1978 [2]. In old age Alma kept to herself at home and was rumoured to swim naked [2]. She died of pneumonia in 1968 and left the house to her two daughters [1]. It was split into four units until novelist Danielle Steel bought it and made it a single home again [2]. Today a towering hedge hides the facade, which Chronicle critic John King called "comically off-putting" [3].

title: Zen in a former synagogue
hook: A Venetian-Gothic synagogue became a Japanese Zen temple, and then the place where Americans first sat zazen with Shunryu Suzuki.
story: In 1895 Congregation Ohabai Shalome, meaning "Lovers of Peace", consecrated a redwood synagogue at 1881 Bush Street. Its facade had Venetian tracery modelled on the Ca' d'Oro or the Doge's Palace [1]. As membership shrank, the building was sold in 1934 to Teruro Kasuga, one of about twenty followers of the Zen priest Hosen Isobe [1]. The Soto Mission was incorporated in 1939. During the Second World War its Japanese American congregation was sent to internment camps, and a Christian group used the building [1]. By the 1950s the Mission had grown to 250 people [1]. In 1959 Shunryu Suzuki arrived from Japan as chief priest. He had no grand plan: he sat zazen every morning in the temple, alone, until American students began to join him [3]. The former synagogue became the place where Westerners first sat with Suzuki, and the first home of the San Francisco Zen Center, until the Center bought 300 Page Street in 1969 [2]. The Redevelopment Agency bought the building in 1973, and the Soto Mission moved to Laguna Street [1]. The old temple is now part of the Kokoro assisted-living centre [1].

title: Four cars down the park steps

place.label: Alta Plaza Park stairs, Clay Street at Pierce

hook: Alta Plaza's grand stairway, built in 1905, still has scars from a 1972 Barbra Streisand comedy that never had permission to drive cars down it.
story: Alta Plaza was set aside as a public square under the 1855 Van Ness Ordinance, though the city didn't hold clear title until 1888 [2]. By July 1905 the Parks Department, under John McLaren, had built four flights of terrace steps up its steep southern side. A few months later, on the morning of April 18, 1906, residents stood on the hill and watched the city burn [2]. The stairway's best-known moment came in 1972. In Peter Bogdanovich's screwball comedy What's Up, Doc?, Barbra Streisand and Ryan O'Neal's characters flee through the city in a stolen Volkswagen Beetle, and the chase takes a shortcut straight down the Alta Plaza steps [1]. The stunt, with four cars crashing down the stairs, wasn't authorised, and it left permanent damage that can still be seen today [1]. Legend has it that it made the city change its film-permit rules, but SFGATE presents that only as legend [1]. The film was a huge hit, earning $66 million on a $4 million budget [1].

title: The Victorian that joined the preservationists
hook: When the last Haas daughter died, her children gave away the family's Queen Anne house to a group formed to fight the bulldozers.
story: William Haas, a Bavarian-born wholesale grocer, built this Queen Anne house on Franklin Street in 1886, to designs by Peter R. Schmidt [1]. It came through the 1906 earthquake and fire [2]. His youngest daughter Alice married Samuel Lilienthal, who led the family business and the Federation of Jewish Charities. They moved in in 1917 [1]. Samuel died in 1957. Alice stayed on in the house until her death in 1972 [1]. San Francisco had only recently seen whole neighbourhoods of the Western Addition flattened for "urban renewal". A new group, the Foundation for San Francisco's Architectural Heritage, had formed in 1971 to fight back, and it had rescued twelve threatened buildings in the largest house-moving project in the city's history [3]. In May 1973 Alice's three children gave the house to that group [1][2]. It became the group's headquarters and a house museum with docent-led tours, and in 2012 the National Trust named it a National Treasure [2].

title: Mammy Pleasant's eucalyptus trees

place.label: Mary Ellen Pleasant Memorial Park, SW corner of Bush and Octavia

hook: Her 30-room mansion is long gone. What remains of one of Gold Rush San Francisco's most powerful Black women is a row of old eucalyptus trees.
story: On March 21, 1974, San Francisco named a row of trees a Structure of Merit, a category the city had used only a handful of times [1]. They stand at the southwest corner of Octavia and Bush. The eucalyptus trees were planted when this was the site of Mary Ellen Pleasant's home, and a plaque in her memory stands among them [2]. Pleasant reached San Francisco around 1852, fleeing prosecution under the Fugitive Slave Law. She cooked for rich families and invested her wages, eventually owning laundries and boardinghouses and building a 30-room mansion at 1661 Octavia [3]. She is credited with giving $30,000 to John Brown before his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry [3]. FoundSF calls her an important western terminus of the Underground Railroad in the 1850s, and says she gained quiet power by placing servants in rich households [2]. Rumours followed her: newspapers and gossip painted her as a brothel keeper and claimed there was a voodoo altar in her basement [3]. Historian Lynn Hudson told the Chronicle she was a woman who "led the Underground Railroad like Harriet Tubman, and amassed a huge fortune, but is largely unknown" [3]. The city proclaimed Mary Ellen Pleasant Day in 2005 [3].

title: A haunted hotel with a magic show

place.label: Chambers Mansion (the Mansions Hotel), 2220 Sacramento Street

hook: An adman bought a rundown Victorian with a gruesome legend, turned it into a haunted hotel with a magic show, and spent years fighting his neighbours.
story: The Chambers Mansion, a Queen Anne built in 1887, came with a gory legend. Chambers's two feuding nieces supposedly inherited it, and one was later found "cut almost in half". NoeHill notes that the story is an urban legend and that even basic facts about Chambers are hard to confirm [2]. In 1977 advertising man Bob Pritikin bought what was by then a rundown boardinghouse. He turned it into an eccentric 16-room hotel and made the most of its haunted reputation [1]. He put on a magic act, the "Pritikin Squished Eyeball Theater", and the Examiner reported that Barbra Streisand and Robin Williams stayed there for a time [3]. Chronicle photographers recorded Beniamino Bufano's grown children setting up his sculpture in 1978, and the demonologists Ed and Lorraine Warren in the billiard room in 1982 [1]. For years the hotel was also a neighbourhood polling place [1]. Not everyone was charmed. From 1979 to 1991 the Chronicle kept reporting on Pritikin's feud with the Pacific Heights Neighborhood Association [1]. The hotel was sold in 2000 and converted to housing [1].

title: Flying buttresses for an earthquake city
hook: Loma Prieta knocked the lantern off St. Dominic's tower. The fix came straight out of the Middle Ages.
story: After 1906 it took St. Dominic's parish more than twenty years to build a permanent home: a huge Gothic church by Beezer Brothers, dedicated on February 19, 1928, before a crowd of more than 2,500 [1]. Its tower was topped by a forty-foot octagonal "lantern" [1]. Sixty-one years later, on October 17, 1989, the Loma Prieta earthquake sent chunks of the upper tower crashing into the street [1]. Much of the painted decoration on the ceiling beams fell and was lost [2]. It wasn't certain the church would be saved. The damaged St. Rose High School building next door was demolished in what Woody LaBounty describes as an apparent compromise between the archdiocese and the city [1]. Pieces of the tower rubble were even auctioned to raise money [1]. The solution was medieval: nine flying buttresses to brace the walls, plus a rebuilt tower. The $6.6 million needed was raised by June 1991, and construction finished in July 1992 [2]. On August 1, 1992, the archbishop rededicated the church, with its new buttresses and shorter tower [1].

title: Flowers for Mrs. Doubtfire

place.label: The 'Mrs. Doubtfire' house, Steiner Street at Broadway

hook: When Robin Williams died, hundreds of San Franciscans didn't go to his home or a theatre. They went to a Pacific Heights doorstep from a 1993 comedy.
story: In Mrs. Doubtfire (1993), Robin Williams plays a father who disguises himself as an elderly nanny to stay close to his children [1]. The family's home in the film is a Victorian house at Steiner Street and Broadway, and both credited screenwriters had Bay Area ties [2]. On August 11, 2014, Williams was found dead at his home in Tiburon. In the days that followed, hundreds of fans came to the Doubtfire house and left flowers, photographs and letters on its steps [1][2]. "There was really no other place for me to pay my respects," 31-year-old Mike Orlick told the Chronicle. "This was the first thing I knew to be comedy" [2]. The house's real owner, plastic surgeon Douglas Ousterhout, told reporters he didn't mind the growing tribute. The Los Angeles Times noted the coincidence that his own work involved surgery for transgender patients, in a house made famous by a man in disguise as a woman [1]. The next night the Giants held a moment of silence for Williams, a regular at their games [1]. For a few days a private front stoop became the city's shrine to him.

title: "Where is Nancy?"
hook: At 2:27 a.m. an 82-year-old man calmly told a police dispatcher that a stranger was waiting for his wife. She understood what he couldn't say.
story: Early on October 28, 2022, David DePape broke through glass-paneled doors at the back of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's Pacific Heights home. He was looking for the Speaker and shouting "Where is Nancy?" [1]. The Speaker was in Washington. Instead her 82-year-old husband Paul woke to find DePape in his bedroom [1][3]. Paul Pelosi said he needed the bathroom, where his phone was charging, and called 911 [1]. On the 2:27 a.m. call he spoke carefully: "there's a gentleman here just waiting for my wife to come back." He gave the address and the intruder's name, and said the man wanted him to put the phone down [2]. Dispatcher Heather Grives sensed that something more was going on and sent a priority call. Police Chief Bill Scott later called her judgement "lifesaving" [1][2]. Officers arrived to find the two men struggling over a hammer. DePape wrenched it away and struck Pelosi before officers tackled him [1]. Pelosi needed surgery for a fractured skull [1][3]. DePape had planned to kidnap and interrogate the Speaker. In May 2024, after his federal conviction for attempted kidnapping and assault, he was sentenced to 30 years in prison [3].
